title: Partner Responsiveness and Insensitivity Predict Emotion Regulation Flexibility in Parent-Adolescent Dyads: A Daily Diary Investigation
description: This study examined how perceived partner responsiveness (PPR) and insensitivity (PPI) predict daily emotion regulation (ER) flexibility, operationalized via the maladaptive ER ratio. Adolescents (N = 112, 12–18 years) and caregivers (N = 108, 33–64 years) dyads completed 28-day diaries. Actor-Partner Interdependence Model (APIM) analyses showed that actor (between and within person) PPR predicted higher ER flexibility, whereas actor PPI predicted lower ER flexibility (ps < .038). Partner higher daily PPR predicted higher ER flexibility (p = .040). Furthermore, role (adolescent/caregiver) moderated the actor daily PPR effect (p = .037) and the partner daily PPI effect (p = .007), revealing distinct relational daily dynamics across roles. These findings highlight how interpersonal attachment perceptions shape daily family ER flexibility.

title: Differential modulation of temporal precision and perceived timing by tactile spatial and temporal context
description: Perception of sensory events depends not only on the stimulus itself but also on the surrounding spatial and temporal context. While contextual interactions have been extensively studied in vision, less is known about how tactile spatial and temporal context shape temporal representation of tactile landmarks embedded within continuous tactile signals. we investigated how neighbouring tactile stimuli influence the temporal precision and perceived timing of a target tactile landmark using an auditory-referenced temporal order judgement task. The number, location, and relative timing of task-irrelevant vibrotactile flankers were manipulated independently. Increasing the number of flankers reduced temporal precision, with comparable effects for adjacent and contralateral stimulation, indicating that temporal precision is limited by contextual interactions beyond local spatial proximity. In contrast, the relative timing of the flankers did not alter temporal sensitivity but systematically shifted perceived target timing. Flankers preceding the target shifted the perceived timing of the target earlier, whereas lagging flankers shifted it to the opposite direction. When one flanker preceded and the other followed the target the direction of the resulting spatiotemporal sequence across the fingers determined the direction of the perceptual bias. These findings reveal two distinct forms of contextual modulation in tactile temporal perception. Spatial context degrades temporal precision, whereas temporal context shifts perceived event timing. These findings demonstrate that spatial and temporal context shape distinct temporal aspects of tactile representations, extending contextual interference from feature identity and localisation to temporal precision and perceived timing.

title: Designing Digital Games to Foster Growth Mindset in PreK–12 Education: A Systematic Review
description:
Background: A growth mindset refers to the belief that abilities and intelligence can be developed through effort, learning, and persistence. Although digital games are often associated with motivational and learning benefits, little is known about how they are intentionally designed to foster growth mindset in preK–12 learners. Understanding how growth mindset principles are operationalized within game mechanics and learning environments is critical for advancing both theory and practice in serious game design.
Purpose: This systematic review synthesizes how digital games have been designed and implemented to promote growth mindset in preK–12 education and examines associated student outcomes and future research directions.
Method: Following PRISMA guidelines, we screened 2,063 records across multiple databases and included 12 empirical studies that explicitly integrated growth-mindset-supportive design elements into digital games. Data were extracted and analyzed to identify trends in study design, targeted competencies, reported effects, and specific game design features.
Results: Most reviewed studies reported positive effects on growth mindset and related competencies (e.g., persistence, creativity, self-efficacy), although some showed mixed or non-significant effects linked to design quality or implementation context. Two overarching design categories emerged: direct supports (e.g., explicit mindset instruction and effort-based rewards) and indirect supports (e.g., adaptive challenges, scaffolding, and mastery-oriented gameplay).
Conclusion: Well-designed digital games hold promise for fostering growth mindset in preK–12 contexts. However, the evidence base remains limited, highlighting the need for more rigorous research designs, longer-term interventions, and deeper theoretical integration to inform scalable and effective game-based mindset interventions.

title: Beyond the Microbiome: Neuroimaging and the Role of Gut Motility in Gut-Brain Interactions
description: Bidirectional communication between the gut and the brain has emerged as a major research focus in recent years, accompanied by increasing use of neuroimaging approaches to investigate how variation in gut microbial composition relates to brain activity, connectivity, and behavior in humans.  In contrast, significantly less human neuroimaging data has examined how the brain contributes to regulation and perception of gastrointestinal motility.  Recently, a growing body of work has begun to investigate how gastric motility relates to neural dynamics in humans. This review aims to address this emerging area by providing a comprehensive overview of experimental approaches that use neuroimaging to quantify the relationship between gut motility, brain activity, and behavior. Specifically, we review three complementary experimental approaches for investigating the role of gut motility in gut–brain interactions: (i) neuroimaging studies comparing dysregulated and healthy gut motility, (ii) perturbation paradigms targeting gastrointestinal signaling pathways, and (iii) studies examining functional coupling between gastrointestinal rhythms and brain activity. Finally, we discuss key open questions and methodological gaps and outline future directions for advancing mechanistic insight into gut–brain signalling.

title: How and for Whom Do Perinatal Depression Interventions Work in LMICs? A Causal Inference and Machine Learning Analysis of Socioeconomic and Psychosocial Drivers
description:
Background: Randomised trials evaluating psychological interventions for perinatal depression (PND) in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) frequently provide conflicting findings. To optimise global maternal mental health interventions, we applied robust causal inference and causal machine learning approaches to individual participant data (IPD) to identify underlying causal mechanisms and responsive subgroups.
Methods: We searched MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, CINAHL, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library from inception to November 19, 2025, for trials assessing the effectiveness of psychological interventions to treat PND. Using IPD, we assessed treatment effect heterogeneity using causal forests, and evaluated causal mechanisms using interventional effects for individual trials and across relevant pooled datasets.
Findings: Seven of 11 eligible studies provided IPD, yielding a pooled sample of 3,154 participants (1,700 intervention, 1,454 control). Heterogeneity analyses of all trials demonstrated top responders presented with higher baseline depression and lower education. A four-study subset incorporating social determinants revealed those with lower perceived social support and education responded best. This four-study subset comprised two two-trial subsets: one delivered by community health workers (CHWs) and one by peers. In the CHW-delivered subset, top responders were similar to the four-study subset; however, within the peer-delivered subset, this effect was negligible. Causal mediation analyses of the four trials revealed social support mediated a 15% symptom reduction. The two-trial CHW subset indicated social support and reduced food insecurity mediated 15% and 3% improvements, respectively. Furthermore, a specific two-trial subset indicated behavioural activation and social support mediated improvements of 32% and 17%.

title: From Seeing to Describing: A Pictogram-based method for investigation the vision-language interface
description:
Visual scenes are routinely transformed into symbolic representations that ultimately become verbal language. However, the cognitive processes underlying this transformation remain only partially understood, largely because visual perception has traditionally been investigated through verbal descriptions that are already constrained by the grammatical organization of language. The present exploratory study proposes an alternative methodological approach by introducing pictogram-based representations as an intermediate level of conceptualization between visual perception and verbal description.
Twenty-four native speakers of Puerto Rican Spanish viewed three experimentally designed visual scenes while their eye movements were recorded using Gazepoint GP3 eye tracker. Immediately afterward, participants described each scene first using pictograms and subsequently through verbal language. 
Qualitative inspection of scan paths revealed substantial variability in visual exploration across participants. In contrast, pictogram selections exhibited considerably greater convergence, suggesting that symbolic representations were not simple reproductions of gaze trajectories. 
Rather than demonstrating the existence of a visual grammar, the present study proposes a methodological framework for investigating how visual scenes become conceptual and symbolic representations before they are fully organized by linguistic structures. The findings suggest that pictogram-based representations may constitute an informative intermediate level for studying systematic visual organization at the vision–language interface.

title: When Does Prayer Promote Flourishing? Attachment, Prayer Profiles, and Psychological Flourishing
description: Prayer is among the most prevalent human behaviors, yet its psychological benefits are inconsistently documented. Most research relies on unidimensional measures and overlooks the relational dynamics that shape the function of prayer. The present study examined associations between attachment to God, latent prayer profiles, and flourishing in a sample of N = 452 Israeli Jews (M age = 44.69, SD = 14.96; 48.0% female). Participants completed the Multidimensional Prayer Inventory (MPI), the Attachment to God Inventory (AGI), and the Harvard Flourishing Measure. Latent profile analysis of MPI subscales identified four prayer profiles: Modal, Disengaged-Habitual, Engaged-Devotional, and Engaged-Penitential. Profiles differed significantly in flourishing and AGI scores: the Disengaged-Habitual profile showed the highest AGI avoidance and the lowest flourishing, whereas the Engaged-Devotional profile showed the lowest AGI anxiety and the highest flourishing. Hierarchical regression revealed that only the Disengaged-Habitual profile predicted significantly lower flourishing relative to Modal prayer, while AGI anxiety and avoidance were the dominant predictors. Interaction analyses showed that  AGI anxiety was less strongly associated with lower flourishing for the Engaged-Penitential profile. These findings underscore the centrality of relational orientation toward God in shaping the psychological function of prayer and inform a person-centered understanding of when and for whom prayer promotes flourishing.

title: Mouse cursor tracking contributes to the psychological validation of the drift diffusion model
description: As a well-established cognitive model of human decision-making, the drift diffusion model (DDM) offers a psychologically intuitive account of the decision-making process by virtue of its four basic parameters. However, the reliance of the DDM on endpoint measures (response times and accuracy) creates a conceptual gap to this process-oriented account, which needs to be bridged with the help of independent process-tracing methods. In this study, we deployed mouse cursor tracking with the aim of validating the psychological interpretation of the basic DDM parameters drift rate, threshold separation, and non-decision time.  In a preregistered replication, 95 participants completed 90 trials of a random dot kinematogram (RDK). Partial least square regression was applied in order to predict the three DDM parameters with the help of 18 cursor measures, which were extracted from the literature. We found support for the psychological interpretation of threshold separation and non-decision time, replicating the results of our previous study, while the analyses of drift rate remained inconclusive. Our results further strengthen our psychological understanding of the DDM, point towards conceptual ambiguities, and encourage further joint application of cognitive models and process-tracing methodology.
